items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1959-06-30
items.q: I remember King Oliver, tall with his horn.

ctx.x: did you recognize any of the guys later? Oh, later on I got to know them like, for instance, like

Black Nolan, Buckeye Wilford. What did they play? They played piano. All these were piano players? They played the blues, yeah, piano players. Black Nolan, Buckeye Wilford. Yeah, they were always welcome. Shine, regular hunky-tunk piano players. First time I heard what it's called now Boogie Woogie. The first time I heard that beat, my little uncle said, look at that guy playing them horses. He used to call it the horses in New Orleans. It wasn't Boogie Woogie, it was horses, because it sounded like a horse's…
Go ahead, it's ready Danny on the second reel.

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So they introduced me to Jelly Roll and King Oliver.

ctx.x: Just had paid for it. A four-string banjo. The kind Kimball had. Kimball was a star around here. I wanted the same kind, and I could play it pretty good. Get to New York with a banjo. I’m around there for about two weeks. While I’m there they take me to the Rhythm Club, Paul and Red Allen. Rhythm Club was where . . . They had about three clubs around there: the Mimo Club, the Rhythm Club, and the Band Box. Three clubs where the musicians hung out at. There, every day I get introduced to different musicians. Paul…

size, but he’s older than me, much older than me. Paul said, “Look out for my nephew, Steele.” Steele said, “All right. I’ll look out for him. Is he all right? Is he wise, or he’s a fool?” Paul say, “He’s not a fool. He’s partly wise, Southern wise.” They kidding and joking. Every day I’d see Steele around, and Steele is showing me all these people. The second day out of there . . . The first day they brought me there, went in the Rhythm Club, there was King Oliver and Jelly Roll [Morton] playing pool. Fletcher…

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: And I went there with him and King Oliver.

ctx.x: And I went there with him and King Oliver. They all were going to see some helluva game. I didn't know nothin' about no baseball. And we went there, and there were all these people. I'd never seen that many people. And we sat up in the top, and I hear him talking about Harry Hooper. Harry Hooper this, Harry Hooper that. He was a White ballplayer who was supposed to have been a sensation, a great center-fielder. Well, that was the music business, see...
Right on 35th Street there, right by the White Sox Park, past... Well, 39th Street was where the Black ballplayers had theirs, over in that same direction -- 39th
Did you know Papa Joe Oliver?
Yes, I knew Joe Oliver. Do you think, I mean, some people,

some people have indicated that he really wanted Louis to stay with him in Chicago when Louis left and went to New York, and that I think Lil Armstrong, his wife, his second wife, sort of had an influence on his leaving the band. Do you think there was any bitterness on Joe's part when Louis left to go to Chicago?
